messages.body_plain:

Hope all is well.

I noticed that DST didn't seem to apply correctly when analyzing data from UK Biobank. Looks like time gets converted correctly to ET but the dates when daylight savings occur get adjusted to US date/time when DST occurs (DST occurs at different dates in UK vs USA).

Meaning a person that wore the device on March 26 and 27th (DST in UK) doesn't seem to have his DST reflected and instead DST comes up on participants that wore the device on March 12 and 13th when DST takes place in the US. I'm flagging DST by looking at discrepancies in spt and sleep duration amounts.

I might be missing something obvious. Any thoughts/ideas?

Thanks,
Pedro

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Single night sleep analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

Thank you very much for your previous reply. It's very inspiring. I am from Sarah's team and we do want to include SPT window detection. So we tried the "RAW" level that you mentioned in your reply on two of our files but we met several problems during the process:
1. we were not able to get the part 5 output
2. we only got one file processed to part 4 output
3. the numbers of part 4 output seemed to be different from what we expected (for example: sleeponset:25.333; wakeup: 26.332; SptDuration: 0.99, we thought that it would be a longer sleep duration)
We wondered if we were doing anything wrong in adding the artificial physical activity data or our codes were wrong. It would be great if you could give us some suggestions regarding it. The files were too large to upload here, so I had to create a google folder for the files (very sorry for the inconvenience): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/15gEtexoOyu6bhs78AwmGhBtg7uFZIDHc?usp=share_link

Our original csv files are (2 files): 7514033122_aligned_data_original and 7514072622_aligned_data_original
Our csv files with added 90-min PA to start and end are (2 files): 7514033122_aligned_data and 7514072622_aligned_data
We used the following codes to process the csv files with added 90-min PA to start and end without sleep log:

library(GGIR)
datadir="V:/.../add_90min_before_after_fake_v2"
outputdir="V:/.../output"

g.shell.GGIR(
  mode=c(1:5),
  datadir=datadir,
  outputdir=outputdir,
  studyname="Attempt1",
  idloc=2,
  f0=1,
  f1=2,
  print.filename=FALSE,
  storefolderstructure = FALSE,
  do.parallel=TRUE,
  overwrite=TRUE,

#part 1#
        windowsizes = c(5,600,600), #windowsizes = c(5,900,3600),
        do.anglez=TRUE,
        chunksize = c(1),
        printsummary=TRUE,

#part 2#
        strategy = 1 , # strategy = 2
        hrs.del.start = 0,          hrs.del.end = 0, #newly added by XZ to fit the one-day pa
        includedaycrit = 0.1, M5L5res = 10, #includedaycrit = 16
        winhr = 5,
        qwindow=c(0,24),
        qwindow_dateformat = "%d/%m/%Y",
        qlevels = c(c(1380/1440),c(1410/1440)),
        ilevels = c(0,36, 201, 707, 8000),
        mvpathreshold = c(201),
        boutcriter = 0.8,
          bout.metric = 6 ,
        epochvalues2csv=TRUE,
        mvpadur=c(1,5,10),
        iglevels = TRUE, #this function calculates intensity gradient

#part3#
        timethreshold= c(5),
        acc.metric="ENMO",
        anglethreshold=5,
        ignorenonwear = TRUE,

#part4#

        def.noc.sleep=1,
        includenightcrit = 1, #changed from 4 to 1
        outliers.only = TRUE,
        relyonguider = FALSE,
        criterror = 4,
        do.visual = FALSE,
        #nnights = 30,

#part 5#
        threshold.lig = c(35.6),
        threshold.mod = c(201.4),
        threshold.vig = c(707.0),
          #Hildebrand 2014 and 2016 intensity thresholds#
        excludefirstlast = FALSE,
        boutcriter = 0.8,
        boutcriter.in <http://boutcriter.in> = 0.9,
        boutcriter.lig = 0.8,
        boutcriter.mvpa = 0.8,
        boutdur.in <http://boutdur.in> = c(10),
        boutdur.lig = c(1),
        boutdur.mvpa = c(1),
        timewindow = c("WW"),
        save_ms5rawlevels = TRUE, #newly added by XZ to save the time series classification (levels) as csv

do.report=c(2,4,5),
dofirstpage=TRUE,
visualreport=TRUE,
viewingwindow=1)

In addition, I also attached the output generated to the google folder as well. Hope it can provide some information. Sincerely thanks again for your time and help.

Julia

Hello,

In the github documentation for Patterson's Verisense step count algorithm, the instructions are clear in saying: "6. Ensure that do.parallel is set to False in the GGIR entry function". I would like to know whether this is still necessary in GGIR.

I ask because in the GGIR documentation for using external functions, it says the following: " Note that, do.parallel is set to FALSE. Unfortunately Python embedding with R package reticulate and multi-threading with R package foreach as used in GGIR do not combine well." This note of caution appears under the section for using an external Python function, whereas the Verisense step count algorithm is using an R external function.

Given the long runtimes necessary for GGIR part 1, being able to run in parallel makes a huge difference. Is there any way this is possible? Thank you in advance for the help and great package!

Thomas Kraft

GGIR does not provide visualizations as the ones you share. The main functionalities of GGIR are related to data processing and extracting meaningful variables related to physical activity, sleep and circadian rhythms from the accelerometer raw signal. Some visualizations are also generated in GGIR, but only as supporting output information, so they are mostly hardcoded and there is not much the user can do to change these visualizations. In your picture attached it seems that the accelerometer raw signal for each axis is plotted, you might just need to read your accelerometer file and try to draw a plot from that data.

2. The graph in the report with the classification of 'light', 'moderate', 'vigorous', 'non-wear' of activity, is also interesting. To achieve this report including this graph the sleep classification steps are taken. This will give me additional information.

I guess you refer to the plot in the folder "results/file summary reports/". These visualizations contains a couple of acceleration metrics calculated in GGIR (not the raw signal as you showed inyour picture), and an approximation to the behavioral classification that is made in GGIR (including the physical activity intensities among other variables). And yes, to get these plots, you need to run all the parts in GGIR, including the sleep detection.

3. In the output folder - meta - sleep.qc that is generated by running the file, there is a document called 'graphyperday_id...' generated. A grey, a yellow, a red, a blue and a black line are illustrated. What does each line mean? Maybe this figure could be of added value to describe the acceleration in each direction.

The colored horizontal lines are the sustained inactivity bouts identified in g.part3, you might want to look at the main vignette <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html> with information on GGIR, its purpose and main functionalities.

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Data validation with ActiLife
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jasmine,

GGIR does not claim to imitate Actilife's MVPA estimates. The only aspect that is replicated is the count calculation and for that we rely on the Neishabouri publication. So, the term validity in the context of MVPA estimates is not applicable here.

There are many decisions to be made in the classification of MVPA that may differ between GGIR and Actilife. Note that there is no universal standard for MVPA classification, by which each software tool has its' own approach. On top of that GGIR does not offer just one estimate of MVPA but gives you as user the freedom to specify the classification as you wish. Therefore, there is no single 'validity' of GGIR to classify MVPA.

Here are a few of the many aspects that may differ in the calculation:

Summed versus average aggregate. In it's default configuration GGIR derives epochs per 5 seconds and in some outcomes averages these per minutes, while Actilife probably takes the sum.
Prep-processing steps that differ, such as auto-calibration, idle sleep mode handling, application of filter, and non-wear detection/imputation.
Algorithm design to classify bouts, such as how to handle gaps in bouts, whether to require that first and last epoch of a bout need to meet the bout criteria, and the order in which inactivity, LIPA and bouts are detected.

Making GGIR comparable to Actilife is further complicated because Actilife is closed source software. So, personally I think it is waste of time to compare MVPA estimates from Actilife with GGIR.

Best,

Vincent
